name: Blessedness identified with divinity (Boethius's pantheistic strand)
plain_explanation: Boethius argues that true happiness (blessedness) and God are ultimately the same thing, so that a person who achieves real happiness has, in some sense, become divine.
precise_definition: The doctrine, in the Consolation, that blessedness and God are both the 'chiefest good' and are therefore identical, so that 'men are made happy by the obtaining of divinity' and 'every one that is happy is a god,' though by nature there is only one God and others are gods only 'by participation.'
why_it_mattered: Russell notes this passes close to pantheism, and 'should have shocked Christians, but for some reason did not' -- an example of how thoroughly Platonic, rather than distinctively Christian, Boethius's philosophical content is.
historical_origin: Developed in the metaphysical portions of the Consolation of Philosophy.
examples: 'They who obtain divinity become gods. Wherefore every one that is happy is a god.'
competing_positions: Orthodox Christian insistence on a strict distinction between Creator and creature
influence_on_later_thinkers: Helped make the Consolation a vehicle for transmitting Platonism into the Middle Ages, especially once later ages supposed (on the strength of theological works of doubtful authenticity attributed to him) that Boethius was securely orthodox.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Theological in vocabulary but philosophically Platonic in substance.
